result.summary: This section collects ancient quotations and testimonia about the Margites, a comic poem attributed to Homer. They describe an old singer arriving at Colophon, the foolish hero Margites who is skilled at nothing, and a proverb about the fox and hedgehog.

scenes.title: Suidas on Pigres
scenes.summary: A lexicon entry names Pigres, brother of Artemisia, as the author of the Margites and the Battle of the Frogs and Mice.

scenes.title: The Singer Comes to Colophon
scenes.summary: An old inspired singer, servant of the Muses and Apollo, arrives at Colophon holding a lyre.

scenes.title: Margites the Fool
scenes.summary: Quotations and a scholiast describe Margites, who knew many things badly, failed at every craft, and was ignorant of his parentage and afraid of his wife.

scenes.title: Fox and Hedgehog Proverb
scenes.summary: A proverb says the fox knows many tricks but the hedgehog's one trick beats them all.

characters.name: Pigres

characters.name: Margites

notable_quotes.reason: Famous description of Margites, the fool who knew many things but all badly.
Origin of the proverb contrasting the fox with the hedgehog, later made famous by Archilochus and Isaiah Berlin.

analysis.text: The fragments portray a comic anti-hero, a fool lacking all skill and common sense, in contrast to the heroes of the Iliad and Odyssey.
Ancient writers attributed the Margites to Homer, though the Suidas entry offers Pigres as author, showing doubts over authorship.

legacy.text: The fox and hedgehog saying became a well-known proverb, later used by Archilochus and in Isaiah Berlin's 1953 essay The Hedgehog and the Fox.

fun_facts.text: Aristotle praised the Margites as a forerunner of comedy, much as the Iliad and Odyssey were forerunners of tragedy.

language_notes.text: Artemisia, wife of Mausolus, ruled Caria and fought in war; Mausolus' tomb gave us the word 'mausoleum'. The bracketed numbers are editor's footnote markers.
'Far-shooting' is a standing description of Apollo, the archer god, who was also patron of music and poetry.
'Knew all badly' means he had wide but poor knowledge, a jack of all trades and master of none.
A scholiast is an ancient commentator whose notes on a text survive; this one comments on a passage of Aeschines.
A proverb contrasting the fox's many tricks with the hedgehog's single defence of rolling into a spiny ball; it echoes the Margites' theme of knowledge.

context_notes.text: Suidas is the name given to a Byzantine Greek lexicon (c. 10th century AD), which includes short biographies of authors.
Colophon was an Ionian Greek city in Asia Minor, one of the places that claimed to be Homer's birthplace.
Aristotle quotes this line in the Nicomachean Ethics when discussing wisdom and practical skill.

literary_notes.text: 'Divine singer' and 'far-shooting Apollo' use traditional epic descriptors, giving the poem a Homeric opening that dignifies the singer.
The gods usually grant skills; here their withholding of every craft marks Margites as a comic fool, setting up the mock-heroic tone.
The compact saying contrasts breadth with one effective skill, in effect the moral opposite of Margites, who knows much but badly.
